title: Acids and Bases: pH and Titrations

standard_text: Strong and weak acids and bases; concentrated and dilute solutions; the ionisation constant of water, Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C; pH = −log[H₃O⁺]; hydrolysis of salts; acid–base titrations, the choice of indicator and the equivalence point; Ka and Kb. meta_desc: Free Grade 12 Physical Sciences worksheets (CAPS): strong and weak acids, Kw, pH calculations, salt hydrolysis, titrations and indicators. 100 questions with answers.
body_html:
How to think about it

A strong acid (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) ionises completely in water; a weak acid (ethanoic acid) ionises only partly, so Ka is small. 'Strong' is about ionisation; 'concentrated' is about how much acid is dissolved. pH = −log[H₃O⁺]; in water at 25 °C, [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1 × 10⁻¹⁴.

In a titration, a standard solution is added from a burette until the equivalence point; then n(acid)/n(base) equals the mole ratio. Salts of a strong acid and a weak base are acidic (choose methyl orange); salts of a weak acid and a strong base are basic (choose phenolphthalein).

Example

[H₃O⁺] = 1 × 10⁻³ mol·dm⁻³. pH?

−log

Answer: 3

Example

Which indicator for ethanoic acid and NaOH?

The salt solution is basic.

Answer: phenolphthalein

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up strong and concentrated.
  • Thinking pH 7 is the end point of every titration.
  • Forgetting the mole ratio for H₂SO₄.

faq.q: Why is a solution of sodium ethanoate basic?
faq.a: The ethanoate ion reacts with water (hydrolysis) to form OH⁻ ions.

faq.q: What is the difference between the equivalence point and the end point?
faq.a: The equivalence point is when exactly the right amounts have reacted; the end point is when the indicator changes colour.
